introduction-the-conversation.core: The shell is a conversation with the operating system. You type a command, the shell parses it (expanding variables, globs and quotes), finds the program on PATH, starts it as a process with arguments, environment and file descriptors 0, 1 and 2, and shows its output and exit status. Fluency comes from knowing that model, not memorising commands: everything composes through text streams, exit codes and pipes.

first_principles.problem: A new engineer copies commands from docs, but when one fails they can't tell whether it was quoting, PATH or the program itself.
truths: Programs communicate via stdin, stdout, stderr and exit codes.

analogy.title: Talking to a precise assistant
analogy.story: They take instructions literally: say exactly what you mean, check their reply, and chain tasks together.
analogy.breaks: Assistants ask clarifying questions; shells don't.

code.text:
f="my report.txt"
rm $f        # tries 'my' and 'report.txt' (word splitting)
rm "$f"      # removes the one file
type ls; echo $?    # builtin/alias/file? and exit status

check.q: Why should variables usually be double-quoted in shell commands?
check.a: To prevent word splitting and glob expansion of their values, e.g. filenames with spaces.

the-core-four-navigation-and-inspection.core: Four habits cover most terminal work. Know where you are and what's there (pwd, ls -la, cd). Read files without opening editors (cat, less, head, tail -f). Find things (find by name, size or time; grep -r by content; locate). Inspect state (df -h, du -sh, free -h, ps, ss). Combined with pipes (| sort | uniq -c | head) they answer most operational questions quickly.

first_principles.problem: A disk-full alert fires and the engineer doesn't know how to find what's using the space.
truths: Most tasks are find, read, inspect.

analogy.title: A detective's basic kit
analogy.story: Map (pwd/ls), magnifying glass (less/grep), fingerprint kit (find) and notebook (pipes).
analogy.breaks: Detectives work slowly; pipes answer in seconds.

code.text:
df -h /
du -xh --max-depth=1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -5
find /var -xdev -type f -size +500M -mtime -2 -exec ls -lh {} +
# found: /var/log/app/debug.log 38G

check.q: Which command shows per-directory disk usage sorted by size?

redirection-and-output-control.core: Every process has file descriptors: 0 is stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr. > redirects stdout to a file (truncating), >> appends, 2> redirects stderr, 2>&1 sends stderr wherever stdout goes (order matters), < feeds a file to stdin, | connects stdout to the next stdin, tee splits output, and /dev/null discards it. Here-docs feed multi-line input. That's how scripts log, filter and silence output precisely.

first_principles.problem: A cron job's errors vanish because only stdout was redirected to the log file.
truths: Pipes carry only stdout by default.

analogy.title: Plumbing with two outflow pipes
analogy.story: Clean water (stdout) and waste (stderr) come out separately; you choose where each pipe leads.
analogy.breaks: Pipes are physical; redirection order changes meaning.

code.text:
./backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1        # both streams appended
./backup.sh 2>&1 | tee -a /var/log/backup.log    # see and save
./noisy 2>/dev/null                              # discard errors only
cat <<EOF > config.ini
[db]
host=localhost
EOF

check.q: What's the difference between 'cmd > f 2>&1' and 'cmd 2>&1 > f'?
check.a: The first sends both streams to f; the second sends stderr to the original stdout (terminal) and only stdout to f.

process-management-ps-kill-and-signals.core: ps aux and ps -ef list processes with PID, parent, user, CPU, memory, state and command; pgrep and pkill match by name; top and htop show live usage. Signals tell processes to act: SIGTERM (15) asks politely to exit, SIGKILL (9) forces it (can't be caught), SIGHUP often means reload config, SIGINT is Ctrl-C, SIGSTOP and SIGCONT pause and resume. Use jobs, bg, fg and nohup or setsid for background work.

first_principles.problem: An engineer uses kill -9 on a database, corrupting in-flight writes that SIGTERM would have flushed.

analogy.title: Asking someone to leave vs removing them
analogy.story: You ask politely (SIGTERM) so they can collect their things; security escorts them out only if they refuse (SIGKILL).
analogy.breaks: People can argue; SIGKILL gives no chance at all.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clean shutdown, force only as last resort.

code.text:
pgrep -a postgres
kill -TERM 4123
for i in $(seq 30); do kill -0 4123 2>/dev/null || break; sleep 1; done
kill -0 4123 2>/dev/null && kill -KILL 4123
kill -HUP $(pgrep -o nginx)     # reload config

check.q: Why should you send SIGTERM before SIGKILL?
check.a: SIGTERM lets the process clean up (flush data, close connections); SIGKILL terminates immediately with no cleanup.

shell-config-bashrc-zshrc-and-the-login-.core: Shells read startup files depending on mode. Login shells (SSH, console) read /etc/profile and ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile (or ~/.zprofile); interactive non-login shells (new terminal tabs) read ~/.bashrc (~/.zshrc); non-interactive scripts read neither by default. Put PATH and environment in profile files, aliases and prompt in rc files, and source ~/.bashrc from ~/.bash_profile for consistency.

first_principles.problem: An alias works in the terminal but not over SSH, and a PATH change works over SSH but not in cron.
truths: Different shell modes read different files.

analogy.title: Arrival briefing vs desk notes
analogy.story: Visitors get a full briefing at reception (login), while desk notes (rc) apply whenever you sit down.
analogy.breaks: Visitors remember briefings; each shell process re-reads files.

code.text:
# ~/.bash_profile
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc
# ~/.bashrc
alias k=kubectl
export HISTSIZE=100000
# crontab: use absolute paths or set PATH
# PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
# */5 * * * * /home/me/bin/sync.sh

check.q: Why does a script work in your terminal but fail in cron?
check.a: Cron runs with a minimal environment (short PATH, no rc files), so commands or variables from your shell config aren't available.

ssh-keys-the-digital-handshake.core: SSH key authentication uses asymmetric cryptography. You keep a private key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519, ideally passphrase-protected) and place the public key in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. On login the server challenges you to sign data with the private key, and the key never leaves your machine. Use ed25519, ssh-agent for passphrases, ~/.ssh/config for hosts and jump hosts, and verify host keys to avoid MITM.

first_principles.problem: A team shares one password for root SSH across servers, and a leaked laptop exposes everything.
truths: Private keys prove identity without sending secrets.
Public keys can be shared freely.

analogy.title: A wax seal only you can make
analogy.story: The server sends a message; you stamp it with your unique seal, and it checks against your registered imprint.
analogy.breaks: Seals can be copied physically; protect private keys with passphrases and hardware tokens.

code.text:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub alice@web1
cat >> ~/.ssh/config <<'EOF'
Host web1
  HostName 10.0.2.15
  User alice
  ProxyJump bastion.example.com
EOF
# server: PasswordAuthentication no, PermitRootLogin no

check.q: Does the private key get sent to the server during SSH key authentication?
check.a: No, only a signature over a challenge is sent; the private key stays on the client.

terminal-multiplexers-tmux.core: tmux runs a server that keeps terminal sessions alive independently of your connection. You can detach and reattach (an SSH drop no longer kills your long migration), split windows into panes, keep multiple windows per session, and share a session for pairing. The key concepts are session, window and pane, and the prefix key (Ctrl-b by default) precedes commands.

first_principles.problem: A 3-hour database migration dies when the engineer's laptop Wi-Fi drops mid-SSH session.
truths: SSH sessions die with the connection.
A server-side process can hold terminals.

analogy.title: A desk you can leave and return to
analogy.story: Your papers stay exactly where you left them even if you go home; you just sit back down.
analogy.breaks: Desks survive power cuts; tmux sessions die if the server reboots.

code.text:
tmux new -s migrate
./run_migration.sh        # long task
# Ctrl-b d  (detach) — or connection drops
ssh db-admin
tmux attach -t migrate    # still running, output intact

check.q: Why run long operations inside tmux on a remote server?
check.a: The session persists on the server, so a dropped SSH connection doesn't kill the running process.
